genres.name: After the Ball
genres.text: Charles K. Harris wrote After the Ball in Milwaukee in 1891, a sentimental song about lost love. He published the sheet music himself and made sure the song was sung in the popular musical A Trip to Chinatown. By 1892 more than two million copies had already been sold. It showed how much money a single song could earn, as long as people heard it often enough.

genres.name: Scott Joplin: Maple Leaf Rag
genres.text: On 10 August 1899, the Black pianist Scott Joplin signed a contract in Sedalia with the publisher John Stark for his Maple Leaf Rag. Ragtime is piano music with a shifted, hopping rhythm. Joplin did not get a one-off sum but one cent per copy sold: royalties. For a Black composer at the time, that was highly unusual. The sheet music sold well for years and made ragtime popular across America.
genres.listen: Listen to how the left hand stays firmly on the beat while the right hand keeps landing just beside it. That shifted rhythm is called syncopation.

genres.name: Tin Pan Alley
genres.text: Around 1900, dozens of music publishers in New York were packed into the same stretch of street: West 28th Street, between Fifth and Sixth Avenue. Every office had a piano, where new songs were tried out all day long. On warm days, through the open windows, it sounded like someone banging on pans. That is how the street got the nickname Tin Pan Alley. Writing songs became a trade here, with an office and a deadline.

genres.name: The Copyright Act of 1909
genres.text: On 4 March 1909, a new copyright law was signed in America. Anyone who put a song on a piano roll or a gramophone record now had to pay the writer and the publisher, for every copy sold. This created mechanical rights. For the publishers of Tin Pan Alley, it was a new source of income. The principle that the writer is paid when his song is spread still applies today.

genres.name: Irving Berlin: Alexander's Ragtime Band
genres.text: In 1911, Irving Berlin wrote Alexander's Ragtime Band, a cheerful song about a band playing ragtime. The sheet music sold more than a million copies. Berlin had come to New York from Russia as a child, could not read music and played the piano on the black keys. Even so, he became one of the most successful songwriters of the century, with songs such as White Christmas and God Bless America.
genres.listen: This is the 1937 version by Louis Armstrong. Listen to how he gives a song of more than twenty years old new life with swing.

genres.name: ASCAP
genres.text: On 13 February 1914, writers and publishers in New York founded ASCAP, an organisation that collects money when their songs are played in public: in restaurants, theatres and later on the radio. A writer could never check that himself. The composer Victor Herbert was one of the founders. Later he won a court case against a restaurant that played his music without paying. In the Netherlands, Buma/Stemra does the same.

genres.name: George Gershwin: Swanee
genres.text: As a teenager, George Gershwin started as a song plugger at a publisher in Tin Pan Alley: he played new songs to customers and performers. In 1919 he wrote Swanee, with the lyricist Irving Caesar. When the famous singer Al Jolson recorded it in 1920, it became Gershwin's first big hit, with an estimated two million records sold. Later Gershwin wrote Rhapsody in Blue and the opera Porgy and Bess.
genres.listen: Listen to how Al Jolson sings with big flourishes, as in the theatre, with an orchestra that follows the rhythm of ragtime.

genres.name: The first Billboard chart
genres.text: On 20 July 1940, the trade magazine Billboard published a national list of the best-selling records in the shops for the first time. Number one was I'll Never Smile Again by the Tommy Dorsey orchestra, with the young Frank Sinatra as singer. It stayed there for twelve weeks. From then on, everyone could see which song was winning. Record labels, radio and jukeboxes began to follow that chart.
genres.listen: Listen to Sinatra's soft, restrained voice above the vocal group The Pied Pipers. A big band that suddenly plays very quietly.

genres.name: BMI and the radio strike
genres.text: On 1 January 1941, ASCAP pulled all its songs from American radio, because the stations no longer wanted to pay. A year earlier, the radio stations had founded an organisation of their own, BMI. BMI signed writers whom ASCAP had ignored: from country, rhythm and blues and later rock 'n' roll. That made room on the radio for music that came from outside Tin Pan Alley.

genres.name: Irving Berlin: White Christmas
genres.text: On 29 May 1942, Bing Crosby recorded White Christmas in Los Angeles in about eighteen minutes, a song by Irving Berlin for the film Holiday Inn. In the middle of the Second World War, many Americans longed for home, and the song struck a chord. It became the best-selling single ever, with an estimated more than fifty million copies. One well-written song could give a writer an income for life.
genres.listen: Listen to Crosby's calm, warm voice, which almost talks. This soft style of singing close to the microphone is called crooning.

genres.name: Rodgers and Hammerstein: Oklahoma!
genres.text: On 31 March 1943, the musical Oklahoma! premiered at the St. James Theatre in New York, the first work by the composer Richard Rodgers and the lyricist Oscar Hammerstein. The songs carry the story forward, instead of standing apart from it. The show ran for more than two thousand performances. At the end of 1943, Decca released the songs, sung by the original cast: the first big cast album. Broadway became a supplier of hits.
genres.listen: Listen to how the show opens with one lonely voice singing about a beautiful morning, without any big spectacle.

genres.name: Les Paul: How High the Moon
genres.text: On 4 January 1951, the guitarist Les Paul and the singer Mary Ford recorded How High the Moon in their apartment in Queens. Les Paul used a tape recorder to stack layer on layer: he played all the guitars himself and Ford sang her voice several times. That is called overdubbing. The record stayed at number one for nine weeks. From now on you could build a record in the studio, instead of just capturing a performance.
genres.listen: Listen for how many more guitars and voices you hear than two people could play at once. Everything is layered.

genres.name: Sinatra and the arranger Nelson Riddle
genres.text: On 30 April 1953, Frank Sinatra worked with the arranger Nelson Riddle for the first time, at Capitol Records in Los Angeles. An arranger decides which instruments play what. Among other things they recorded I've Got the World on a String, a song from 1932. It became a hit and Sinatra's career, which had stalled, got going again. An old song suddenly sounded fresh through a new arrangement.
genres.listen: Listen for the short, sharp stabs of the brass and the swing underneath. Above it, Sinatra sings relaxed and self-assured.

tracks.title: I've Got the World on a String

genres.name: Leiber and Stoller
genres.text: Jerry Leiber and Mike Stoller were nineteen when they wrote Hound Dog in 1952 for the blues singer Big Mama Thornton. Elvis later made it a worldwide hit, and they also wrote Jailhouse Rock for him. They also arranged the recordings themselves, as one of the first independent producers. With The Coasters they made funny hits such as Yakety Yak in 1958. Their way of working became the example for the young writers around Broadway.
genres.listen: Yakety Yak is about a teenager who has to tidy up for his parents. Listen to King Curtis's saxophone, which answers like a fourth voice.

genres.name: The Billboard Hot 100
genres.text: On 4 August 1958, the first Billboard Hot 100 appeared. Until then, Billboard had separate charts, for example for sales in shops and for what DJs played. The Hot 100 merged everything into one chart of a hundred songs. The first number one was Poor Little Fool by teen idol Ricky Nelson. The Hot 100 still exists and is the best-known chart in the world.
genres.listen: Listen to the simple guitar and the backing vocals: this is what a teenage hit sounded like in 1958.

genres.name: Aldon Music and 1650 Broadway
genres.text: In 1958, Don Kirshner and Al Nevins started the publishing house Aldon Music in the building at 1650 Broadway, close to the Brill Building. They hired young writers, often couples, who wrote songs for teenagers in small rooms with a piano: Carole King and Gerry Goffin, Barry Mann and Cynthia Weil, Neil Sedaka and Howard Greenfield. The Brill Building became the name for this whole way of working.

genres.name: Motown: the assembly line
genres.text: In January 1959, Berry Gordy started a record label in Detroit with 800 dollars from his family. Gordy had worked on the assembly line of a car factory himself and organised Motown in the same way: writers wrote, a fixed house band played, artists were taught posture and dress, and every week a meeting decided which recordings were good enough. Office and studio shared one house.
genres.listen: Money (That's What I Want) by Barrett Strong from 1959 was one of the first hits for Gordy. The lyrics are exactly about what it was all about: money.

genres.name: Will You Love Me Tomorrow
genres.text: On 30 January 1961, Will You Love Me Tomorrow by The Shirelles was number one in America, the first song by a girl group to top the Hot 100. It was written by Carole King and Gerry Goffin, a young couple at Aldon Music: King was only eighteen. The lyrics ask a strikingly direct question: will he still love me tomorrow, after tonight? It was the duo's first big success.
genres.listen: Listen to the strings and the calm, rolling accompaniment: a small drama of less than three minutes.

genres.name: Little Eva: The Loco-Motion
genres.text: Eva Boyd was the babysitter of Carole King and Gerry Goffin. Because she could sing well, she recorded the demo of The Loco-Motion, the trial recording with which writers tried to sell a song to a performer. That demo sounded so good that it was released as a single, under the name Little Eva. On 25 August 1962, the song was at the top of the American chart. Writing and releasing were very close together.
genres.listen: Listen to the handclaps and the girl explaining how to do the dance. A demo that became a worldwide hit.

genres.name: The Beatles write their own songs
genres.text: On 22 March 1963, Please Please Me, the first album by the Beatles, was released. Of the fourteen songs, eight were their own. Bands and singers who wrote their own songs, such as the Beatles and Bob Dylan, made the Brill Building model old-fashioned. Who still wanted to sing a song by an office writer? Carole King and Goffin saw their commissions decline. King later started singing herself.
genres.listen: Please Please Me was written by Lennon and McCartney. Listen to the harmonica and the two-part singing.

genres.name: Phil Spector: Be My Baby
genres.text: What the writers in New York came up with was often recorded elsewhere. Producer Phil Spector worked in Los Angeles with a fixed group of session musicians, later called the Wrecking Crew. He stacked guitars, pianos, strings and echo into a wall of sound. Be My Baby by The Ronettes from the summer of 1963, written with Ellie Greenwich and Jeff Barry, is the textbook example. The producer became a star.
genres.listen: Hal Blaine's drum intro, three dull beats and a hard crack, is one of the most copied ever. Then the wall opens up.

genres.name: Bacharach and David
genres.text: In 1964, Walk On By by Dionne Warwick became a hit, written by the composer Burt Bacharach and the lyricist Hal David at the Brill Building. Bacharach used unusual changes of time signature, jazz chords and melodies that go surprisingly up and down. Warwick was one of the few who sang his difficult songs effortlessly. Together they made dozens of hits, and their songs were sung by hundreds of artists.
genres.listen: Listen to Warwick's soft voice, the trumpet and the strings. The chorus has an unexpected melody that stays in your head.

genres.name: Holland-Dozier-Holland
genres.text: On 22 August 1964, Where Did Our Love Go by The Supremes was number one, written and produced by Brian Holland, Lamont Dozier and Eddie Holland. In a few years, the trio wrote dozens of hits for The Supremes and The Four Tops. The house band, the Funk Brothers, played on almost all Motown records, usually without credit on the sleeve. After a dispute over money, the three left Motown in early 1968.
genres.listen: The rhythm is a foot stamping on a plank: every beat equally heavy, easy to dance to. Diana Ross sings low, the others answer with baby, baby.

genres.name: George Martin and Yesterday
genres.text: On 17 June 1965, producer George Martin recorded a string quartet at Abbey Road studio for Yesterday, a song that Paul McCartney had recorded alone with his guitar. A string quartet is two violins, a viola and a cello. The other Beatles did not play. Martin, who was classically trained, wrote the arrangement together with McCartney. This is how the producer helped the band go beyond guitar, bass and drums.
genres.listen: Listen to how the strings only come in after the first verse, and that there are no drums to be heard.

genres.name: I Heard It Through the Grapevine
genres.text: Norman Whitfield and Barrett Strong wrote I Heard It Through the Grapevine, and Whitfield recorded it several times with different artists. Marvin Gaye's version was not allowed to come out as a single by Motown boss Berry Gordy and ended up on an album. Only when DJs started playing it did it become a single after all, in October 1968. It became the best-selling Motown single until then. The boss had been wrong.
genres.listen: Listen to the menacing start with electric piano and Gaye's tense voice, singing that he heard it through the grapevine.

tracks.title: I Heard It Through the Grapevine

genres.name: Motown moves
genres.text: In 1972, Berry Gordy moved Motown from Detroit to Los Angeles, where he wanted to make films. Artists such as Marvin Gaye and Stevie Wonder had just forced through that they could make their own music. The time of the assembly line was over. The old house in Detroit later became the Motown Museum. Studio A is still there, just as it was in the sixties.

genres.name: ABBA: Waterloo
genres.text: On 6 April 1974, ABBA won the Eurovision Song Contest in Brighton with Waterloo. The writers were Benny Andersson and Björn Ulvaeus, with their manager Stig Anderson. They had listened closely to Phil Spector and British glam rock. In the years after, they made hit after hit in Stockholm, with a sound that worked in every language, sung by Agnetha Fältskog and Anni-Frid Lyngstad. Sweden became a country of hits.
genres.listen: Listen to the piano, the saxophone and the chorus that sticks at once: a battle as a love story.

genres.name: ABBA: Dancing Queen
genres.text: On 16 August 1976, Dancing Queen by ABBA was released. After a piano glissando, the song does not begin with a verse but with a piece of the chorus: You can dance, you can jive. The listener gets the strongest moment straight away. Only then comes the verse about a Friday night on the dance floor. It was ABBA's only number one in America. Benny and Björn worked like a hit factory of their own.
genres.listen: The chorus starts before the verse. A hit that begins at its strongest point.

genres.name: Quincy Jones and Thriller
genres.text: On 30 November 1982, Thriller by Michael Jackson was released, who had started at Motown. Producer Quincy Jones had songs written by Jackson himself and by writers such as Rod Temperton, and had the best session musicians of Los Angeles play, including members of Toto. It became the best-selling album of all time. The producer was now just as important as the artist.
genres.listen: Jackson wrote Billie Jean himself. Listen to how the drums and bass make a tight, creeping rhythm from the very first beat.

genres.name: Stock Aitken Waterman
genres.text: In March 1985, You Spin Me Round by Dead or Alive was number one in England, the first big hit by Mike Stock, Matt Aitken and Pete Waterman. Waterman wanted to make a British Motown. Their studio in South London worked like a factory: a fast, tight rhythm, a bouncing synthesizer bass and a chorus that stuck at once. The press called it The Hit Factory.
genres.listen: Listen to the stomping bass, like a machine, and the deep voice of Pete Burns.

genres.name: Jimmy Jam and Terry Lewis: Control
genres.text: On 4 February 1986, Control by Janet Jackson, Michael's youngest sister, was released. Producers Jimmy Jam and Terry Lewis only wanted to work in their own Flyte Tyme studio in Minneapolis, so Janet travelled to them. Together they wrote hard, tight songs with drum machines and synthesizers. The album reached number one. Jam and Lewis became one of the most successful writing and producing duos in R&B.
genres.listen: Listen to the hard, dry hits of the drum machine and the short synthesizer chords. Everything sits tight on the beat.

genres.name: Bananarama: Venus
genres.text: On 6 September 1986, Venus by Bananarama was number one in America. It was a new version of a 1969 hit by the Dutch band Shocking Blue. The three singers wanted to turn it into a dance song and knocked on the door of Stock Aitken Waterman. They hesitated at first, but gave in. The hit factory from South London now had a number one in America too.
genres.listen: Listen to how Shocking Blue's guitar riff has been replaced by a fast synthesizer and a tight drum machine.

genres.name: Rick Astley: Never Gonna Give You Up
genres.text: On 27 July 1987, Never Gonna Give You Up by Rick Astley was released, who had first worked as an assistant in the Stock Aitken Waterman studio. His deep voice surprised the public: anyone who heard him expected a much older man than the 21-year-old in the video. The song reached number one in 25 countries. Twenty years later it got a second life as an internet prank: rickrolling.
genres.listen: Listen to the tight drum machine, a Linn 9000, and the synthesizer bass that bounces cheerfully up and down.

genres.name: Kylie Minogue: I Should Be So Lucky
genres.text: Kylie Minogue was known in Australia as an actress in the soap Neighbours. When she came to London in 1987, Stock Aitken Waterman turned out to have forgotten that she was coming. There was no song ready. According to the story, Stock and Aitken wrote I Should Be So Lucky in about forty minutes, while she waited outside. In February 1988 it was number one in England.
genres.listen: The song is about someone who is only lucky in love in her dreams. Listen to how the chorus stays in your head at once.

genres.name: Roxette: The Look
genres.text: On 8 April 1989, The Look by the Swedish duo Roxette was number one in America. That was down to an exchange student from Minnesota, who took the CD with him from Sweden and handed it in at the radio station KDWB in Minneapolis. The station played the song, and other stations followed. After ABBA, Roxette proved once more that Sweden could make English-language worldwide hits. Songwriter Per Gessle wrote it.
genres.listen: Listen to the raw guitar riff and the short, loose phrases. The lyrics sometimes sound like nonsense, but you keep singing them.

genres.name: Band Aid II
genres.text: On 3 December 1989, Stock Aitken Waterman recorded a new version of Do They Know It's Christmas? in their London studio, for the famine in Ethiopia. Bob Geldof asked them, because they then dominated the British charts. Kylie Minogue, Jason Donovan, Cliff Richard and Bros sang along. The single was number one for three weeks at Christmas. It was a high point of the hit factory from South London.
genres.listen: Listen to how the solo voices take over from each other line by line above a typical SAW rhythm of drum machine and synthesizers.

genres.name: Denniz PoP and Cheiron
genres.text: In 1992, the Swedish DJ Denniz PoP started the Cheiron Studios in Stockholm. He produced All That She Wants by Ace of Base, which reached number one in many countries in 1993. Denniz PoP was not a trained musician, but knew exactly what a hit needed. He took young writers under his wing, among them the metal singer Martin Sandberg. He would become known as Max Martin.
genres.listen: All That She Wants mixes reggae with pop and a dark synthesizer melody. Listen to how bare and tight everything sounds.

genres.name: Timbaland and Aaliyah
genres.text: On 26 May 1998, Are You That Somebody? by Aaliyah went to American radio, written by Static Major and producer Timbaland. Timbaland built a rhythm full of stuttering clicks and silences, and added a giggling baby from a sound effects record. The song became a big radio hit. Timbaland showed that the producer with a strange sound of his own could be just as recognisable as the singer.
genres.listen: Listen to the baby sound and the rhythm that keeps stopping and shooting off again. Sing along on the beat: it is harder than you think.

genres.name: Max Martin: ...Baby One More Time
genres.text: Max Martin first wrote ...Baby One More Time for the Backstreet Boys and the American group TLC, who both turned it down. Then it went to the sixteen-year-old Britney Spears, and it was released in October 1998. By hit me, Martin probably meant something like call me one more time. The song became a worldwide hit. Denniz PoP, his mentor at Cheiron, did not live to see the success: he died in August 1998.
genres.listen: The song opens with three heavy piano notes and then straight away the voice: Oh baby, baby. The hook is there in the first seconds.

genres.name: Melodic mathematics
genres.text: In April 1999, I Want It That Way by the Backstreet Boys was released, written by Max Martin and Andreas Carlsson. Martin works with melodic mathematics: every line of lyrics has about as many syllables as the line that rhymes with it, long high notes carry vowels that sing well, and the hook returns as often as possible. What the words mean is less important. The group themselves said the lyrics are not entirely logical.
genres.listen: Listen to how the vowels on the high notes are open, as in way. The lyrics are vague, but it sounds like a big feeling.

genres.name: Stargate: Irreplaceable
genres.text: On 17 October 2006, Irreplaceable by Beyoncé was released. It was made by the Norwegian production duo Stargate, with singer Ne-Yo as lyricist. Ne-Yo had first meant it as a country song. Stargate and Beyoncé turned it into an R&B song, with the acoustic guitar still up front. It was number one in America for ten weeks. Just as in Sweden, American hits now also came from Norway.
genres.listen: Listen to the acoustic guitar under the beat: a trace of the country song it first was.

genres.name: Rihanna: Umbrella
genres.text: In March 2007, Umbrella by Rihanna was released, written by Terius The-Dream Nash and Christopher Tricky Stewart, with Kuk Harrell and Jay-Z. It was first offered to Britney Spears, but her record label let it go. That is how songs travel from artist to artist in the hit factory. Umbrella was number one in many countries and became one of the best-known songs of the decade.
genres.listen: The post-chorus is one word in pieces: ella, ella, eh, eh. A second hook on top of the first.

genres.name: Spotify
genres.text: On 7 October 2008, Spotify opened to the public, a streaming service from Stockholm by Daniel Ek and Martin Lorentzon. Streaming means that you play music over the internet without buying the file. Spotify made deals with the big record labels, so that the music was legal. Later this became the main way to listen to music. That also changed how hits are made and counted.

genres.name: The writing camp
genres.text: In March 2010, Rihanna's record label held a writing camp in Los Angeles. It rented a series of studios for two weeks and had dozens of writers and producers work on songs at the same time: one had lyrics, another beats. About two hundred songs came out of it, eleven of which ended up on the album Loud. Man Down was written there. Such a camp is expensive, but quickly produces a lot of material.
genres.listen: Listen to the reggae rhythms in Man Down: at a writing camp, writers also try styles that the singer has not done before.

genres.name: Adele: Someone Like You
genres.text: In January 2011, Someone Like You by Adele was released, from the album 21. She wrote it with the American songwriter Dan Wilson, in two days. The song uses the same chord progression as Let It Be, I-V-vi-IV, but in A, and the piano plays the chords as a rolling movement. After a performance at the Brit Awards it became a number one in England and then in America.
genres.listen: Listen to the piano that plays each chord as separate notes one after another, an arpeggio, under Adele's voice.

genres.name: Taylor Swift and Max Martin
genres.text: On 18 August 2014, Shake It Off by Taylor Swift was released, written with Max Martin and Shellback. Swift came from country and made her first real pop album, 1989, with the Swedes. Martin by now had a studio of his own and a team of younger writers, just as Denniz PoP had once trained him. He rarely gives interviews, but is behind dozens of number-one hits.
genres.listen: Listen to the saxophone and the cheerleader rhythm with handclaps. A country star going completely pop.

genres.name: The Blurred Lines case
genres.text: On 10 March 2015, a jury in Los Angeles ruled that Robin Thicke and Pharrell Williams had infringed Marvin Gaye's Got to Give It Up with their hit Blurred Lines. They had to pay Gaye's family millions of dollars. According to many musicians, they had not copied a melody, but mainly the feel, the rhythm and the sound. Songwriters were alarmed: could you still build on an old style?

genres.name: Hits get shorter
genres.text: In 2017, researchers at Ohio State University published a study of the American top 10 since the eighties. The average intro had shrunk from more than twenty seconds to about five. On streaming services, a stream only counts after thirty seconds, and listeners skip quickly. That is why the hook comes earlier and earlier, and songs get shorter. The way of distribution changes the shape of the song.

genres.name: Old Town Road and TikTok
genres.text: On 13 April 2019, Old Town Road by Lil Nas X reached number one in America. He bought the beat online for thirty dollars from the Dutch teenager YoungKio. On the app TikTok, millions of people made videos with the song, and so it became a hit before a major record label did anything with it. It stayed at number one for nineteen weeks, a record. Short videos became a new route to the chart.
genres.listen: Listen to the banjo from the sample and the heavy 808 bass underneath: country and hip hop at the same time.

genres.name: The Weeknd: Blinding Lights
genres.text: On 29 November 2019, Blinding Lights by The Weeknd was released. The credits list five writers, among them Max Martin and Oscar Holter. The song sounds like a record from 1985: a synthesizer riff as intro and a drum machine with the sound of the eighties, the Stock Aitken Waterman formula in a new guise. In 2021, Billboard declared it the most successful song in the history of the Hot 100.
genres.listen: The song opens straight away with a synthesizer riff that is a hook in itself. Compare it with Never Gonna Give You Up.

genres.name: The Ed Sheeran case
genres.text: On 4 May 2023, a jury in New York decided that Ed Sheeran had not copied Let's Get It On, the song by Marvin Gaye, with Thinking Out Loud. The heirs of co-writer Ed Townsend had sued him. In court, Sheeran said that chord progressions belong to everyone. After the Blurred Lines case, many songwriters felt relief: a widely used chord sequence is not property.
genres.listen: Listen to the calm chords under Thinking Out Loud and compare them with Let's Get It On. Are they similar enough to speak of copying?

genres.name: Max Martin beyond Lennon
genres.text: Measured in number-one hits on the American Hot 100, Max Martin is the most successful songwriter ever after Paul McCartney; he has by now overtaken John Lennon. Even so, the general public hardly knows his face. He rarely gives interviews and almost never appears on a stage. That fits the tradition of the hit factory: from Tin Pan Alley and the Funk Brothers to the Brill Building, the makers often stayed behind the scenes.
